newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Blacks see apartheid unpunished in Malan case.
newsitem.headline: Blacks see apartheid unpunished in Malan case.

text.p: Many black South Africans saw the Malan case as a trial of the hated apartheid system itself, and with the acquittal of all the defendants they wonder if they will ever see justice for crimes of the past.

Hardline apartheid defence minister Magnus Malan and 19 co-defendants, from white generals to alleged black henchmen, were cleared on Thursday and Friday of responsibility for the massacre nine years ago of 13 children, women and men at a prayer meeting.
If the past is a slow-healing wound for South Africa, the acquittals have rubbed in salt.
The verdict has again pitted those linked to the old white regime against most blacks, along the familiar old battle lines, and dented the progress of racial reconciliation.
Both sides and the judge agree only on one thing: that the state prosecution case was fundamentally flawed.
Malan and his allies say this was because the charges were ludicrous in the first place.

"The legal grounds on which the prosecution was based were flimsy and somewhat far-fetched," said National Party leader F.W. de Klerk, who has apologised for apartheid but said he, as the country's last white president, had done nothing wrong.
"The accused should never have been charged and they have been done an injustice," he added.
But some blacks said the outcome was instead a sign of flaws in a justice system that is demoralised, underpaid and relies on white judges and prosecutors who took office under apartheid.
"In the eyes of our people this verdict may not be acceptable," President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress said in a statement.
"The prosecution team failed them. This will have far- reaching consequences. It is doubtful whether our people will ever have confidence in the judicial system."

Mandela, who has devoted his life to reconciliation between South Africa's long-divided races, expressed his support for the courts and vowed that police would not cease to hunt down those responsible for secret apartheid-era death squads.
He is far more forgiving than most. Blacks in Durban said the case had robbed them of hope of justice.
"There is no way now I can feel reconciliation," said Mbusi Ntuli, whose brother, an ANC sympathiser, was the intended target of the massacre.

The most important political trial of the post-apartheid era has also sharpened animosity between the ANC and Mangosuthu Buhelezi's Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party. The judge blamed unnamed Inkatha members for the massacre.

Some 15,000 people have died in a decade of warfare between the two groups, at last dying down, for control of communities in Inkatha's power base, KwaZulu-Natal province. Some political analysts said they feared the verdict could stir trouble again.
Inkatha leaders said the trial was politically motivated to embarrass Buthelezi, Mandela's main black rival, and said ANC members should stand trial for the murder of Inkatha supporters.

South Africa's independent Human Rights Committee (HRC) said the Malan verdict had negative implications for Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which hopes apartheid-era criminals will confess before it and repent.
In return for penitence, the perpetrators are offered amnesty, but fewer than expected have come forward.
Malan defied the commission, saying he was innocent and would prefer to clear his name in court. He won.
"This result probably means that some perpetrators will decide instead to take their chances with the legal system," the HRC said. Tutu's commission said it would be studying the trial.
Tutu has started to summon reluctant former generals and leaders of the apartheid regime to appear before him, saying the time had come to reveal the iron fist within his velvet glove.
But their lack of goodwill, and reports that the army is still shredding sought-after evidence, have soured his mission to lay the past to rest before his commission finishes up by early 1998.
By then, electioneering will be under way for polls the next year, Mandela will be winding down from public life and, optimists hope, a new forward-looking era will have begun.
